title: Exact chemo--thermal Metropolis Brownian engine: chemical leverage, temperature-neutral stall, power optimization, and multicyclic dissipation
abstract: We develop an exactly solvable chemo--thermal extension of the three-state Metropolis Brownian heat engine. The particle moves through the periodic energy sequence $0\to E\to 2E\to0$, performs mechanical work against a load $f$ on every forward step, interacts with two cold links and one hot link, and consumes one fuel molecule of free-energy drop $\muu$ on the hot transition. Local detailed balance gives an exact cycle affinity \begin{equation*} \mathcal A=E\left(\Tc^{-1}-\Th^{-1}\right)+\muu/\Th-f\left(2/\Tc+1/\Th\right), \end{equation*} and the full stationary probabilities and current are obtained without linear-response, weak-driving, or high-barrier approximations. Several results follow. First, the exact stall force is \begin{equation*} \fs=\frac{E(\Th-\Tc)+\Tc\muu}{2\Th+\Tc}. \end{equation*} Second, there is a temperature-neutral chemical compensation point $\muu_*=3E/2$ at which $\fs=E/2$ for every $\Th>\Tc$ and the hot and cold heats both vanish at reversible stall. summary: This work provides an exact theoretical framework for a chemo-thermal Brownian engine, modeling energy conversion driven by both temperature gradients and chemical fuel. Key findings include determining the stall force and identifying a unique temperature-neutral point where performance is robust against temperature changes. The methodology is highly valuable for understanding non-equilibrium processes in complex open systems.
main_problem: The paper develops an exactly solvable model to study energy transduction in a chemo-thermal Brownian heat engine, driven by both temperature gradients and chemical free energy drops.
main_result: It derives the exact stall force and identifies a temperature-neutral chemical compensation point where the stall force is independent of reservoir temperatures. The analysis also shows that the stationary current increases monotonically with chemical fuel consumption.
method: The analysis uses the master equation approach derived from local detailed balance to obtain exact stationary probabilities and currents, avoiding common approximations like linear-response theory.
model_or_system: The system is a three-state periodic energy sequence engine ($0 	o E 	o 2E 	o 0$) coupled to two cold and one hot reservoir, with chemical fuel ($\mu$) consumed during the hot transition.
key_observables: Cycle Affinity ($\mathcal{A}$), Stall Force ($f_{stall}$), Stationary Current ($J$), and Exergy Efficiency ($\eta_x$).
important_parameters: Temperature difference ($\Th - \Tc$), energy gap ($E$), and chemical potential drop ($\mu$).
main_assumptions: The analysis is exact for the unicyclic case, though a multicyclic extension is introduced later. The Metropolis dynamics are assumed.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the universal intersection of stall curves at the temperature-neutral point, the monotonic increase of current with chemical affinity, and the dependence of power on the mechanical load.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the model and derives the exact cycle affinity and stall force. It then analyzes the temperature-neutral point and the current's dependence on chemical potential. Finally, it discusses the power optimization and extends the analysis to multicyclic operation.
why_interesting: The rigorous, exact treatment of non-equilibrium thermodynamics in a coupled chemo-thermal system provides powerful analytical tools applicable to open quantum systems where multiple energy reservoirs (heat, chemical potential) drive dynamics.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Three-state chemo–thermal Metropolis engine. The cold bath acts on links 1 ↔2 and 3 ↔1; the hot bath acts on 2 ↔3. A forward hot transition consumes one fuel molecule of free-energy drop ∆µ. Each clockwise jump advances the particle by one lattice spacing against load f.
FIG. 2. Exact stall force versus chemical free energy for sev- eral hot/cold temperature ratios, with E = Tc = 1. All curves cross at the temperature-neutral point ∆µ/E = 3/2, fstall/E = 1/2.
FIG. 3. Exact stationary current versus chemical affinity for several loads (E = Tc = 1, Th = 2, Γ = 1). The dotted hori- zontal lines are the strong-chemical-driving limits in Eq. (88).

FIG. 4. Exact operating-mode map for Th/Tc = 2. The solid line is stall, the dashed line is qh = 0, and the dotted horizontal line is qc = 0. The three forward-running colored regions correspond to a hybrid heat engine (qh > 0, qc > 0), a chemical motor dissipating into both baths (qh < 0, qc > 0), and a chemical motor that also refrigerates the cold bath (qh < 0, qc < 0).

FIG. 5. Exact current and mechanical power versus load for several chemical affinities (E = Tc = 1, Th = 2, Γ = 1). Chemical driving moves stall to larger load and increases the maximum power. The dots indicate numerical solutions of the exact stationarity condition (100).
